This framework is built upon three key assumptions: the conditional independence of modalities given a bridge modality, the ability of contrastive learning with the InfoNCE loss to model the correct density ratio, and specific properties of the representation distribution (either uniform or Gaussian). Under these assumptions, the authors derive closed-form expressions for the marginal probability ratio, demonstrating that the similarity between representations of unpaired modalities can be used to estimate this ratio. The paper further proposes a practical Monte Carlo approximation algorithm, based on this theoretical framework, to estimate the marginal probability ratio between unpaired modalities. This algorithm is presented as a way to combine pre-trained models or handle language ambiguity in reinforcement learning. The authors validate their theoretical findings through experiments on synthetic data and real-world datasets, demonstrating the effectiveness of their approach in multimodal alignment tasks. The use of Bayesian reasoning and the connection to probabilistic graphical models further enhance the theoretical depth of the work. This algorithm is a valuable contribution, as it provides a way to combine pre-trained models and handle language ambiguity in reinforcement learning.
